title: OpenTelemetry for Claude Code and the Agent SDK: signals, traces and content gates
titleVi: OpenTelemetry cho Claude Code và Agent SDK: tín hiệu, dấu vết thực thi và kiểm soát nội dung

units.text: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
What you will be able to do
Wire metrics, log events and traces from Claude Code or the Agent SDK to an OTLP collector, and explain why enabling telemetry alone exports nothing
Choose a backend type suited to each signal and control metric attributes such as session.id to manage cardinality
Read a trace to find where a run spent its time and tokens, including subagent spans
State what telemetry redacts by default and which variable reveals prompts, responses, tool details, tool output or raw API bodies
Key concept
Three opt-in OpenTelemetry signals

Claude Code and the Agent SDK emit three separate signals: metrics (counters), log events (one structured record per thing that happened) and traces (timed spans). Each signal has its own exporter variable, and a signal with no exporter never leaves the process, whatever else you turn on.
In this lesson
Metrics, log events and traces answer different questions
Controlling what metrics carry
Reading a trace: spans across a run and its subagents
Telemetry content gates: redacted by default
Metrics, log events and traces answer different questions

Monitoring an agent in production comes down to three questions. How much are we using, and what does it cost? What exactly happened on this request? Where did this run spend its time? Claude Code and the Agent SDK answer each one with a different OpenTelemetry signal, and each signal has its own exporter.
Metrics
are counters for tokens, cost, sessions, lines of code and tool decisions, so they suit totals and rates.
Log events
are structured records for each prompt, API request, API error and tool result, so they answer "what happened".
Traces
are spans for each interaction, model request, tool call and hook, so they show where the time went.
Each signal, how it is enabled, and the backend types it suits
Signal
Enable with
Suited backends
Metrics
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER (otlp, prometheus, console, none)
Time series databases for rate calculations and aggregated metrics; columnar stores for complex queries and unique-user analysis
Log events
OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER (otlp, console, none)
Log aggregation systems for full-text search and log analysis; columnar stores for structured event analysis
Traces (beta)
OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER plus CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1
Distributed tracing systems for span visualization, request waterfalls and latency analysis
A full-featured observability platform can hold all three. It earns its place when you need to correlate them, for example to jump from a cost spike in a metric to the events and spans behind it.
Exporting takes several switches, and each one is a place for a CI rollout to go silently wrong.

Checkpoint 3 of 7
Exam question

A platform engineer sets CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 on every CI runner but the team's OTLP collector never receives any spans, metrics, or logs from Claude Code jobs. No other telemetry variables were configured. What is the most likely cause of the missing data?
The collector rejects every signal until CLAUDE_CODE_ENHANCED_TELEMETRY_BETA=1 is also set, regardless of which exporters are chosen
Telemetry is enabled but no exporter was selected, so OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER and OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER default to producing no export at all
The CLI only emits telemetry once the console exporter has been configured first as a required local fallback
The organization's Admin API key must be exported through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS before the CLI will emit any signal

Raising OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL reduces the number of time series a metrics backend stores.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 4 of 7
Check yourself

A platform team's metrics backend bill has grown sharply. Each of roughly a thousand short-lived CI jobs a day shows up as its own time series for the same Claude Code token counter. The team still wants to break usage down by deployment.environment, which they set through OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. Which single change cuts the series count without losing that breakdown?
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=false
Raise OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL from 60000 to 300000 so the series are flushed less often
Set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_TEMPORALITY_PREFERENCE=cumulative
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID=false
Checkpoint 5 of 7
Exam question

A metrics backend's bill spikes because every exported time series carries a unique session.id, fragmenting cardinality across thousands of short-lived CLI sessions. The team still needs cost and token totals broken down by model. Which change addresses the cardinality problem without losing the model breakdown?
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID=false so session.id is dropped from exported metrics while other attributes like model remain
Disable the metrics exporter entirely and reconstruct cost and token totals later from the Usage and Cost Admin API
Increase OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL to reduce how often metrics are flushed, which lowers the number of unique series produced
Switch the Usage API bucket_width parameter from 1h to 1d so the Admin API aggregates sessions before they reach the metrics backend

Reading a trace: spans across a run and its subagents
A trace turns one turn of the agent loop into a tree. The root is
, which runs from the prompt arriving to the response. Under it, each call to the Claude API is a
span, and each tool invocation is a
span. A tool span has two children:
for the permission wait and

for the work itself. That split is the first thing to check when a turn feels slow. A long wait span means a person was approving a prompt, not that the tool was slow. A subagent is a separate agent that the main session spawns, with its own model requests and tool calls, and the Agent tool is the tool call that starts one. The subagent's own
and
spans nest under that Agent tool's span.

Checkpoint 6 of 7
Check yourself

Users say one agent turn took about 40 seconds. In the trace, the claude_code.tool span for a Bash call lasts 39 seconds. Its claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user child takes 37 seconds and its claude_code.tool.execution child takes 2 seconds. What is the most likely cause of the delay?
A person took a long time to approve the tool's permission prompt
The model request behind the tool call was retried several times
The model's output was cut off by max_tokens, so the turn stalled
The Bash command itself ran slowly, so the tool needs optimizing

Telemetry content gates: redacted by default
By default, telemetry records the shape of the work and not its content. Prompts are reduced to their length, and the interaction span's
attribute reads

. Assistant responses are reduced to their length too. Tool arguments, tool output and raw file contents are left out. Each kind of content has its own gate, and the gates send data only to the endpoint you configure, never to Anthropic. That still means a collector you run will be holding source code and secrets once a gate is open. One field is present without any gate: under OAuth,
appears in telemetry attributes, so filter it in your backend if that matters to you.
Predict first
A team sets OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 to audit what developers ask Claude Code, and leaves every other content variable unset. What do assistant_response events now carry?
The full response text as well, because the responses gate falls back to the prompts gate
Only the response length, because responses have their own gate
Nothing at all, because assistant_response events need tracing enabled
Content gates, from narrowest to widest
Variable
What it reveals
OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1
Prompt text on user_prompt events (in both prompt and prompt_text) and on the claude_code.interaction span
OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES=1
Response text on assistant_response events; inherits OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS when unset
OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1
Tool parameters and input: Bash commands, file paths, URLs, MCP server and tool names, skill names; real names on cost and token counters
OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1
A tool.output span event with file contents, Bash output and MCP/WebFetch/WebSearch results; requires tracing
OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES
Full Messages API request and response JSON, including the entire conversation history; 1 for inline, file:<dir> for untruncated bodies on disk
Two details catch out redaction rules. First, masking prompt text in a collector has to cover both
and
. Second, under detailed beta tracing the
span carries model output in
, and that attribute follows

, not the responses gate. Raw API bodies are the widest gate: turning them on counts as consent to everything the prompt, tool-detail and tool-content gates would reveal. Inline content is truncated at
, which defaults to 61440 UTF-16 code units (60 KB) so values fit backends that cap attributes at 64 KB.
On the exam

Managed settings are the settings an administrator deploys and enforces across all Claude Code users; developer-set values are the ones individuals choose themselves. When managed settings set OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, Claude Code removes every developer-set per-signal endpoint, so a developer's endpoint never wins. Exporter selectors are not removed. They follow normal per-key precedence, so a developer's own selector value can still switch a signal to none or console unless you set the selectors in managed settings as well.
Exam trap
Turning on OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS exports prompts only; responses stay redacted until their own flag is set.
Why is that wrong?
